newsitem.title: USA: Report criticizes FBI lawyer's White House dealings.
newsitem.headline: Report criticizes FBI lawyer's White House dealings.

text.p: A U.S. Justice Department internal investigation released on Friday chastised the FBI's top lawyer for poor judgment in his dealings with the Clinton White House on the FBI background files controversy.

The report by the department's Office of Professional Responsibility found that General Counsel Howard Shapiro, a longtime associate of FBI Director Louis Freeh, made "a very serious mistake and exhibited very poor judgment."

But the internal watchdog unit concluded in the 29-page report that Shapiro's actions did not rise to the level of professional misconduct and had not been motivated "by any alleged personal or political ambitions."

Freeh said in a statement the report will be referred to an FBI board to consider what, if any, disciplinary action should be taken. A final decision on any disciplinary steps will be made by the deputy attorney general, he said.

The report comes at a time when relations between the FBI and the White House have been especially strained as Freeh last month refused to give the White House details of China's alleged efforts to influence U.S. political campaigns.

FBI sources said Shapiro, a former prosecutor and law professor, soon would leave the FBI, mainly out of concern that his staying would hurt Freeh. He has been considering several offers to go into private law practice, they said.

Shapiro said in a statement he was "gratified" the report found he did not engage in any misconduct or wrongdoing and that he had not been motivated by "any personal ambitions" or "any political agenda."
White House spokesman Mike McCurry declined comment on the report, calling it an internal Justice Department review.

The investigation began after last year's disclosure that Shapiro alerted the White House about politically damaging information in an FBI background file on former White House personnel security chief Craig Livingstone.

Shapiro tipped off the White House's counsel's office on July 15 about a 1993 report in the file that said Livingstone had been recommended for his job by first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton. She has denied any role in his hiring.
The report said his action "exacerbated a political problem by contributing to the appearance that the FBI, and particularly Shapiro, was not sufficiently independent of the White House."

Congressional investigators arrived at FBI headquarters to inspect the file on July 16, but by then Shapiro had sent two FBI agents to the home of agent Dennis Sculimbrene, who wrote the report, to question him about it.
The report criticised Shapiro for authorising the interview.

Investigations were underway then by Whitewater special prosecutor Kenneth Starr and congressional committees into the White House's obtaining of hundreds of secret FBI background files, including some on prominent Republicans.
The report rebuked Shapiro for a lack of coordination with Starr and "faulty conjecture" in assuming the Livingstone hiring question was outside Starr's interest.
Shapiro in February gave the White House another tip by providing it with a draft copy of the book "Unlimited Access" by Gary Aldrich, a former FBI agent assigned to the White House.

The book alleged that Clinton aides had used drugs and were sexually promiscuous, citing late-night mysterious disappearances by President Bill Clinton himself. The allegations involving Clinton have been discredited.
The report said Shapiro in providing the draft copy was carrying out a decision at least tacitly endorsed by Freeh.
